title: fix K/V DMA geometry and eligibility bounds for models with fewer than 8 KV heads
author: positron-mark
head: 3a8544cd353e9197cdc46bc327a14ab638d41dfd
body:
## Why

Running ingested qwen3-30b-a3b with hardware attention failed on the very first forward pass with
`Encountered NaN s_star`. It happened at tp2 and tp4, from a 16-token prompt upward. Every other hardware
attention model we run has 8 KV heads; qwen3-30b has 4, and it was the first model to exercise that
difference.

The cause was in how the K cache is written to the FPGA. The hardware reserves a fixed slot for each token:
room for 8 KV heads of 128 elements, regardless of what the model actually has. The code that writes K
assumed the slot was only as wide as the model's KV head count. With 8 heads the two agree. With 4 heads,
the second, third and fourth tokens in every block of four were written to the wrong place, and the FPGA
read K values that had never been written. V was already laid out for 8 heads, which is why the failure
showed up in the softmax denominator rather than in the attention output.

Fixing that and testing it at 4 heads surfaced a few related problems, all fixed here as separate commits:

- The V write path had its own geometry bug. The "readback fence" (the word the host waits on to know a
  DMA has landed) was placed based on the transfer length instead of the row size, so at 4 heads it pointed
  past the bytes being written. Production does not use the fence, but the tests do.
- Several helpers silently clamped an unsupported KV-head count instead of rejecting it.
- A model with 32 or more query heads per KV head would pass the hardware-eligibility check and then abort
  at runtime, because a 5-bit command field cannot hold that ratio.
- The debugging code that reads K back from HBM used the wrong geometry too, and nothing in the tree
  compiled it, so it had rotted unnoticed.

This is unrelated to the `NaN v_star` failure seen in the field on 8-head models.

## What changed

**K cache DMA.** Positions within a block are now stepped by the hardware's fixed slot size. The transfer
still carries only the heads the model has. This is the fix for the qwen3 failure and it changes nothing for
8-head models.

**V cache DMA.** The transfer length and the readback fence are now both derived from the block's row
layout, so the fence always sits inside the bytes the DMA writes. Production behavior is unchanged.

**Rejecting unsupported shapes.** Every K and V transfer helper now asserts that the KV-head count is
between 1 and 8 instead of clamping it. The eligibility check that decides whether a model may use hardware
attention now also requires `n_heads / n_kv_heads <= 31`, which is what the 5-bit `gqa` field can hold.
A shape past that limit takes software attention instead of aborting on the first hardware command. The
runtime assertions and the worker reference the same constant, so the limit is defined once.

**K cache readback (debug only).** The reader now inverts the exact layout the writer produces, so a dump
of a model with 64-wide heads is no longer scrambled. The dump header is compiled by one test target so
future drift is caught at build time.

**Documentation.** The hardware attention doc now says K is written as one contiguous descriptor per token
(splitting by head across FPGAs is planned, not implemented) and has a corrected V layout table. Two helpers
carry doc comments answering questions raised in review: why one keeps a `head_size` parameter production
never varies, and that the other is test-only.

## How it was tested

**Batch test at 4 and 8 KV heads.** `t_hwattention_batch` now runs its whole battery at both head counts.
To make a wrong K write visible, the test first fills every K slot with a poison value through the 8-head
path, then writes the real K through the path under test. K is filled so that each query has a known
correct maximum score; if any slot still holds poison, that maximum comes back wrong. The unused V rows are
poisoned the same way and the attention output is checked against the source values. K and V are loaded
using the same descriptor path production uses, so the test covers the code that actually runs in serving,
not only the blocking helper.

Each fix was proven red/green on hardware by temporarily restoring the old behavior:
- Old K stride: the 8-head case passes, the 4-head case fails every query with the poison value.
- Old K descriptor path in the test: the previous test still passed with a broken production stride (that
  was the gap); the new test fails 4768 checks, every one reading the poison score.
- Old K readback: the round-trip test fails at the third element of a 64-wide head.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: add initial DMA coalescence for KV_hwcacheblock transfers
author: mcherba
head: 7f80aa17da20f6c0ce1dd456653b9b8f5a79d257
body:
Initial work to try coalescing DMA transfers for runs of KV cache within a layer like we create during prompt parsing.

## Descriptor tradeoff

For a 128-token prompt block, the expected K+V data-descriptor count is shown below. The V side has 32 descriptors per window; the K side has one descriptor per GOF in the window.

| Coalescence tokens | Windows per 128 tokens | K+V descriptors per 128 tokens |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 | 16 | 544 |
| 16 | 8 | 288 |
| 32 | 4 | 160 |
| 64 | 2 | 96 |
| 128 | 1 | 64 |
commit_subjects: add initial DMA coalescence for KV_hwcacheblock transfers
formatting
Improve V path handling to reduce extra work as per https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4128#issuecomment-5498556672
Replaced cooperative drain vectors with bounded std::array batches and immediate empty-queue exits in model.hpp.
Consolidate prepared-transfer grouping and dispatch into one helper
clean up DMA teardown for coalesced descriptor paths
Address Review feedback

inline.body:
xfer_gofs does some avoidable per-call work on the prefill critical path (a 4096-token 36-layer prefill runs this ~4608 times):

- gof.cpp:37 — the ctor memsets the whole batch allocation (up to 128 KiB), but in the common 8-head/128-head-size config the populate loops below overwrite every byte. Zeroing is only needed for the padded regions (kv_head_size < HW_BAKED_HEAD_SIZE, n_kv_heads < 8/odd). ~576 MB of dead stores per long prefill plus cache pollution.
- gof.cpp:256+ — six heap vectors per call (pieces/specs/bases/fetchers/qdatas/qlens); the sibling xfer_gof uses fixed stack arrays. Sizes are bounded by coalesce_gofs*(1+FETCHERS_PER_DEVICE), so stack arrays work here too.
- gof.cpp:278 — the std::sort of pieces is avoidable: emit K in fetcher order and V fetcher-major and the vector is sorted by construction.

Related, one level down: the V populate at gof.cpp:333 is piece-major, so v_head_fn runs its full head gather into the shared v_buf once per (fetcher,pos,head) — 1024 calls per GOF vs 32 in the gof::populate path this replaces — and the caller reads only head_size/32 of each gather. Inverting to (gof,pos,head)-outer and scattering with the packed writes shuffle_v_entry_padded already implements removes the 32x. That also matters for correctness margin: v_buf is per-(gal,position) but layer-agnostic while staging_busy is per-(gal,layer), so two workers batching different layers of one gal race on v_buf — a pre-existing window, but this widens it ~32x.

Two decode-path costs in the drain helpers:

- Here (and wait_for_coop_gof at :2993): the std::vector<gof_coop_task> is constructed and reserved before checking whether the coop queue has anything. These run from the hw_q_released_layer spin and begin_attention_job — per worker, per layer, per decode token — and the queue is almost always empty there, so this adds a malloc/free per spin iteration where the old code try_dequeued with zero allocation. Try-dequeue the first task before allocating (early-return on empty) and collect into a fixed std::array — task_budget is bounded by max(4, coalesce_gofs).
- gof_rodeo_impl_batch (:3114) re-asserts the kv_complete_fn condition fire_gof_rodeo already asserted on identical inputs. TRON_ASSERT is compiled into release, so every decode-path GOF completion pays 8 std::function invocations instead of 4. Keep one copy.

Also worth a look while in here: the 'prompt-sized pass' predicate at :2970 counts token jobs, so a decode pass co-batching >=32 sessions also gets the escalated budget of 8 — contradicting the comment that generation keeps the small fairness budget, and at the worst spot (pre-barrier idle point, all attention workers serialize behind the unlucky one). Gating on an explicit pass-shape signal instead of a token count keeps decode at 4 and won't silently re-tune if hwkv_coalesce_tokens changes.

This sort/group/dispatch block now exists in four near-verbatim copies:

1. backfill_shard, count==1 branch (here, gof.cpp ~471-490)
2. backfill_shard, batch branch (gof.cpp ~491-515)
3. gof_rodeo_impl_batch, count==1 branch (model.hpp ~3136-3160)
4. gof_rodeo_impl_batch, batch branch (model.hpp ~3161-3185)

All four carry the same safety-critical sequence from the staging-lifetime work in #3928: reservation.commit() -> guard.commit() -> tracker.push(pending_xfer{...}), where the ordering is what keeps staging alive under submitted descriptors (the explanatory comments for that ordering only survive next to some of the copies). The two sites also carry twin hand-written request structs (prepared_xfer in model.hpp is backfill_request plus a shard member) and two copies of the run-grouping predicate (same layer, consecutive gof_in_shard, same coalesce window — rodeo adds same-shard).

Any future change to the commit ordering, the grouping predicate, or a pending_xfer field has to be mirrored in all four places, and a missed copy would be a silent staging-lifetime bug rather than a compile error.

This singleton V-gather scratch is insufficiently aligned.
     gof.cpp:436 introduces an ordinary stack array, then passes it through v_head_into_fn to page::get_v(). That gather uses _mm256_store_si256, requiring 32-byte alignment.

This affects singleton decode submissions and singleton remainders during backfill or fragmented batching. Compiling the changed function confirmed that its scratch can be misaligned by 16 bytes. A small UBSan reproducer using the  gather’s exact intrinsics fails with that alignment and passes with an aligned destination.

Fix: add alignas(HWCACHEBLOCK_ALIGN_BYTES), matching the batch scratch, and exercise the real gather through singleton population. Current optimized Clang can mask the violation by fusing instructions

**Coverage gap: the new tests cannot detect incorrect DMA destinations.**

`pos_fake::xfer_n_blocks` (`src/pos/fake.cpp:336–346`) discards every descriptor argument. These tests inspect selected staging values and descriptor counts, so incorrect HBM bases, fetchers, source offsets, or transfer lengths would still pass. Both new batch cases also start at GOF index zero.

Please extend an existing CI suite to observe the descriptors at the transfer boundary and verify that coalesced transfers write the same bytes to the same HBM locations as singleton transfers. Include nonzero GOF indices, partial coalescence windows, and runs on either side of a page boundary. That would protect against silent KV corruption from descriptor construction errors; the current packing assertions do not establish that contract.

**Coverage gap: the changed rodeo orchestration is bypassed by the focused tests.**

The added tests call `shard::xfer_gofs` directly. Even the existing test named "gof rodeo populates and xfers to shard" manually invokes population and transfer. Those cases do not exercise the new cooperative batching path or `dispatch_prepared_gof_xfers` grouping and reservation handoff.

Please extend an existing CI suite with focused cases using the production dispatch/drain path: mixed shards and layers, a reservation collision leaving a gap in an otherwise consecutive run, and branch fanout. Assert that each eligible target receives the correct KV exactly once, skipped positions remain untouched, and the forward-end drain finishes all outstanding submissions before scheduler-owned job storage can be rebuilt. These are missing safety-contract checks; I have not observed a lost-GOF or premature-completion failure in the implementation.

issue_comments.body:
I seemed to notice the V-populate path doing a lot of extra work in these changes. So I prompted Claude with that (and told it to look at the PR overall). I also asked it to evaluate any collateral concurrency risks... below are those results:

  - **Top robustness item** — batch teardown is unsafe by default (dma_tracker.hpp): dropping a queued batch pending_xfer without a manual abandon() frees the buffer under live DMA; only dma_tracker::clear remembers today. Also nothing asserts the gof-pin and batch-pin fields are mutually exclusive. Fix: abandon-in-destructor unless completed, plus an XOR assert in push().
  - **Heavy-concurrency risk** — decode at ≥32 users escalates the drain budget 4→8: the "prompt-sized pass" test counts token jobs, so co-batched decode qualifies; up to 8 populate+submit rounds at a pre-barrier idle point serializes the attention workers. Gate on pass shape, not token count.
 - **Hot-path costs:** you were right about this. The V-populate path does 32x the work now of the path it's replacing... batch V populate re-runs the full head gather 32× per element consumed (and widens a pre-existing cross-layer v_buf race window by the same factor); each batch does a redundant up-to-128 KiB memset + 6 mallocs + an avoidable sort; help_drain_gof now mallocs per call in decode spin loops; the kv_complete assert loop runs twice per decode GOF.
  - **Branching trees:** shard-fanout now populates and pins one batch buffer per shard instead of sharing one staging population.
  - **Consistency nits:** batch path lacks the n_kv_heads ≤ HW_MAX_KV_HEADS assert every sibling writer carries — parity, not a live bug since  eligibility gating keeps over-wide models off the HW path; and it uses % FETCHERS_PER_DEVICE where the single path spells % dev->num_fetchers — moot given the  32-fetcher design invariant, but worth spelling the same way.

title: Attention: skip ranges without software work
author: BillBaumann
head: 9653307d687d49c7d5a9a5989902697bc1a69fce
body:
Skip per-query scans of attention pages already covered by hardware offload. Preserve software tails and partial-page visibility, and fix Pending readiness checks for pages shared by multiple writers.

**Large reductions in Ready worker time during both prompt and generation; no material overall model speedup demonstrated.** GPT-OSS-120B TP4, one user at 32K context, hardware attention enabled:

| Phase | Reduction in summed Ready worker time |
| --- | ---: |
| Prompt / prefill | **76.7%** (2.64 → 0.614 s) |
| Generation / decode | **37.3%** (29.6 → 18.6 ms) |

Within Ready sections with no estimated software work, the reductions are **99% for prompt** and **47.9% for generation**. These are overlapping worker spans, averaged across three matched trace pairs. Repeated untraced model checks at 2K and 32K, including four users at 2K, show equivalent throughput and latency (less than 1% difference).

**Potential gain:** removing these scans frees workers and may improve model performance when CPU attention becomes a bottleneck. That larger benefit has not been measured.

**Pending sections:** the increase reproduces at **2.14% more prefill worker time** across three fresh pairs (+3.05%, +2.03%, +1.35%), versus **5.2%** in the original single pair. Generation Pending averages **2.65% more worker time**, driven by one pair (+6.72%; the other two are within 1%). These are summed worker times; no corresponding full-model latency or throughput regression has been measured. Pending generally contains new pages requiring computation. The readiness fix waits for every writer of a readable physical page and deduplicates checks for consecutive tokens sharing that page.

Validation:

- `t_llama_unit`: 128,487 assertions / 30 cases; `t_ranged_mask`: 262 assertions / 25 cases. Both passed at 1, 2 and 4 slices; benchmark metadata is refreshed.
- Restoring only the old producer-token visibility predicate makes both shared-page readiness cases fail; the other 29 cases pass.
- Pinned clang-format-19, applicable Lefthook checks and `make build-test` passed.
- CI: [host tests](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/actions/runs/34655835716/job/103452391973) **92 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed**, including the proxy suite; [FPGA tests](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/actions/runs/34655835716/job/103452392013) **53 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed**. All 19 checks in that CI run passed.

Performance checks used clean, frozen Nix `cross-avx512` RelWithDebInfo builds and the same GPT-OSS-120B TP4 plugin, weights and prompt tokens. Both ran through public Distributed Dice wrappers on **andoria-cf8c, NUMA0**, with NUMA1 idle for the primary comparisons. Hardware attention was enabled at engagement 127; sliding-window layers retain software attention. No live-token or per-user prompt-chunk override was set.

One-user sweeps used three isolated iterations per version, the same 32K→2K runtime order, 32,769 / 2,049 actual input tokens, 128 generated tokens. The four-user CI-style control used 2,048 input tokens per user, 514 generated tokens. Multi-user samples average the four correlated request measurements within each fresh batch.

Reversing run order and extending the four-user control to ten isolated iterations did not reproduce a consistent generation slowdown. Raw model measurements are preserved in the recorded artifacts.

Three fresh matched trace pairs use GPT-OSS-120B TP4, one user, 32,769 input tokens and 128 generated tokens, with alternating base/head order. With `--trace-passes 249-264` and categories `-*,+model,+scheduler,+hwattention`, all six included captures have **zero loss and zero incomplete slices**: eight 128-query prefill forwards, the final one-query prefill forward, and seven decode forwards. One incomplete capture was excluded and replaced.

| Traced work | Mean summed worker time (ms), base → head | Change (lower is better) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |

title: Report prepare stalls once per device
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
head: 4d9ee3b24fe22a79620601fa1f22aac8866630f6
body:
The prepare-ring-full diagnostic uses a function-static flag shared by devices whose prepare mutexes are distinct. Parallel prepares can race on that flag, and the first device to stall suppresses diagnostics from other devices.

Store `prepare_stall_reported` on `PosDevice`, protected by the existing `hw_prepare_mutex`. Each device reports its first full-ring stall independently. The flag starts false when the device is constructed; the wait loop and diagnostic contents are unchanged.

title: kv_cache: load last_print_bytes with a valid memory order
author: jhan-positron
head: 4b98dc134aaf88ceb7b42b232a431bd245c7cadd
body:
Two commits: the one-line fix, and a regression test for it in the existing `t_llama_unit` binary.

**The fix.** `log_kv_footprint`, the function in `h/tron/models/kv_cache.hpp` that prints the throttled "KV cache footprint" log line (KV = the attention keys and values the server caches), loaded its `last_print_bytes` atomic (a counter several threads update) with `std::memory_order_release` (a memory order: the rule for how the operation is ordered against other memory operations; release is meant for stores). The C++ standard does not allow that order on a load: the precondition of `atomic<T>::load` ([atomics.types.operations]) is that the order is neither `memory_order::release` nor `memory_order::acq_rel`. The old call therefore had undefined behaviour. The loaded value only decides whether the footprint has changed enough to print the line again. The two totals in the same function (`total_bytes`, `total_books`) are already updated with relaxed operations. The load is not used to synchronise access to other data. The load therefore becomes relaxed; the store that follows keeps its release order.

Pre-existing on `main` (line 454 at a80b102c18). Ben (bgamari-positron) pointed at it while reviewing #3879 ([comment 3937077542](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/3879#discussion_r3937077542), anchored at line 487 of the head 60d66d9c04, where the same load sits inside that PR's version of the function). Separate PR so the fix does not depend on the AMX (Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions) attention change.

**The test** (first test case in `t/t_llama_unit.cpp`, a fake host test that needs no model files; placed there at the reviewer's request instead of in a binary of its own). The wrong and the right order compile to the same instructions with clang, so no check on program output can fail; the compiler, clang-tidy, ThreadSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer are silent too. The detector is libstdc++'s own precondition check inside `std::atomic::load`, enabled by `_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` on the `t_llama_unit` target only (`add_catch_test ... DEFINES _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` in `t/CMakeLists.txt`). The macro is independent of `NDEBUG` and changes no linkage names, sizes or layouts, so the checked test object links against the unchanged `libtron`. The check reaches the load because `log_kv_footprint` is always-inline (`TRON(inline)`) and is called from the constructors of the KV books (a book is one allocation of cache pages) that this translation unit already instantiates: the test file compiles its own checked copy, and a wrong order aborts (SIGABRT, the abort signal) at the first call. The new case forks a child through the file's existing `assertion_signal` helper (fork, run the callable, report the signal that killed the child, 0 for none), calls `tron::log_kv_footprint(1, 0)` there (1 byte is below the 1 GiB print granularity, so nothing is logged), and requires 0. Without the fix the case fails (`REQUIRE(... == 0)` sees 6 = SIGABRT); with the fix it passes. The case is declared first on purpose: the binary runs as one ctest test in declaration order, and with `main`'s line 13 of the 27 existing cases construct a book unisolated and abort the whole process, so the fork-isolated case reports the contract by name before that happens. The `#error` at the top of the file makes a dropped define a build failure instead of a test that can no longer fail. The bug entered `main` in 0b5bdf2c86 (2025-04-10).

Effect of the define on the 27 existing cases, measured on delphi-3bda (Xeon 6962P, one socket, mean of three runs each): all 27 pass, no other precondition check aborts, run time 6.38 s to 6.51 s (+2 %, inside the 0.26 s spread of the three baseline runs), peak RSS unchanged at 640 MiB; the control build without the define also passes. The `t_llama_unit` rows in `config/test-benchmarks.json` are left as recorded: the +0.13 s is smaller than the spread already inside the granite_rapids_6962p row (3.38 s to 3.64 s), and a refresh needs a whole-machine `bin/slice bench --update`.

Verified on delphi-3bda (Xeon 6962P, clang 19, the project's CMake preset): at this head `t_llama_unit` passes (28 cases, 120,057 assertions); the same tree with the fix reverted fails the new first case (`6 == 0`) and then aborts in the first book-constructing case with the libstdc++ message (exit code 134).

Labels: `Skip benchmarks`.

title: page_share_counters: count query tokens per KV page visit (instrumentation, default off)
author: jhan-positron
head: ef13273ba9c354c6c5ce4e02735f95541daf9634
body:
This PR is the first piece of breaking up PR #3879. This PR is based on `main` and does not depend on the other breakup pieces.

## What it adds

`h/tron/kernels/page_share_counters.hpp` and five hook blocks guarded by `TRON_PAGE_SHARE_COUNTERS` in `h/tron/models/self_attention.hpp`. For every page visit - a page visit is the processing of one (KV page, kv_head) pair in the software attention loop - the hooks count the query tokens which have relevant K tokens, keep a histogram of it (slots are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5-8, 9-16, >16 query tokens) and add the per-call totals to process-wide counters. Visits without any relevant K tokens are not counted. At normal process exit, a static object's destructor prints the summary to stderr if at least one visit was counted.

The CMake option `TRON_PAGE_SHARE_COUNTERS` (top-level `CMakeLists.txt`, default OFF) adds the define of the same name to the `tron` library. Without the define the header declares no instrumentation and the preprocessor removes the five hook blocks, so a default build compiles no counter code into the library. The new test supplies the define to its own translation unit.

The CI build job leaves the option OFF, so the runtron it bundles as the benchmark artifact carries no instrumentation. The weekly coverage preset (CMakePresets.json, built by cpp-coverage.yml) sets it ON, so the hooks are compiled there and exercised by t_llama_unit.

## What does this PR serve?

Following is from example runs (qwen-3-4b, tp2 = tensor parallelism over two FPGA cards, attention on the CPU, 8 users). The numbers are workload-wide averages; they show how often several query tokens visit the same page, which is the condition under which a per-page kernel could serve several query tokens from one page load:

| Workload (8 users) | Query tokens per page visit, average |
|---|---|
| prefill-heavy: prompt 2048 tokens, 2 generated | 110.9 |
| decode-heavy, private prompts: prompt 64 tokens, 512 generated | 1.02 |
| decode with a shared system prompt: 1024 shared + 64 private prompt tokens, 256 generated | 5.06 |

The kernel in the next PR serves one query token (its four query heads) per page load. The counters tell where batching several query tokens per page load would help (prefill, shared prompts) and where it would not (private decode: 1.02 query tokens per visit).
The counter instrumentation, behind an option, makes the measurement repeatable when the batching behavior changes. A query counts as long as at least one K token on the page is relevant to it; the counters do not measure whether the page was dense (all 64 tokens visible) for that query.

## Review history

Ben [asked why the counters are global inline variables](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/3879#discussion_r3936847383) and then [named the C++17 feature himself](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/3879#discussion_r3937150401): a C++17 inline variable may be defined in every translation unit that includes the header, yet the program has exactly one object with one address, so the instrumentation needs no .cpp file.

The agent review Wade (Wado-posi) posted on #3879 ([comment](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/3879#issuecomment-5544513215)) asked for the instrumentation to leave the tree; this PR keeps it behind an option with a test and a stated purpose instead.

## Verification

Built and tested on 2026-09-08 on delphi-3bda (Intel Xeon 6962P, a Granite Rapids CPU) in a clean worktree, CMake preset cross-avx512 (with -DBUILD_INGEST_MODELS=OFF, which only skips the ingest models), once with -DTRON_PAGE_SHARE_COUNTERS=ON and once with -DTRON_PAGE_SHARE_COUNTERS=OFF (the default). 

In both configurations the two test targets and the tron library they link compiled, and Catch2 (the test framework) printed t_page_share_counters "All tests passed (61 assertions in 4 test cases)" and t_llama_unit "All tests passed (120054 assertions in 27 test cases)". In the ON build t_llama_unit printed the four [page-share] lines at exit; in the OFF build it printed none. clang-format-19 (the repository's formatter) leaves the files unchanged. 
The cost-data entry for t_page_share_counters has not yet been measured, so CI's "Check slice cost data" step fails until it is added to config/test-benchmarks.json. Update 2026-09-08: that entry is now in commit 6c735e63ae (measured on delphi-3bda with bin/slice bench --update: 0.698 / 0.700 / 0.696 s and 8 MB peak memory at the 1-, 2- and 4-slot placements).

## Labels

`Skip benchmarks`, the repository's default for every PR.

title: Split software attention pages across cores by query (for small page and large query counts)
author: BillBaumann
head: a9a9cf30a4acdfcd76276fae64931bde358e9b90
body:
Parallelize software attention within a page when hardware offload or sliding windows leave too few pages to keep cores busy. Workers process disjoint query ranges in both Ready and Pending phases, preserving each query's full-page reduction and section-completion accounting.

Split only single-page sections with at least 32 relevant queries, when productive page/KV-head tasks number at most half the workers. The planner accounts for worker load, speed, and setup/join overhead; it requires a 10% predicted improvement and chooses the fewest pieces within 3% of the best predicted completion time.

Measured GPT-OSS prompt throughput improves **2.38% at 2K** and **4.28% at 32K**; generation improves **1.03% at 32K**. Llama controls are equivalent to main in both phases. Changes under 1% are reported as equivalent.

| Model | Users / instances | Prompt / gen tokens | Prompt throughput | Gen throughput |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| GPT-OSS 120B TP4, HW attention on | 1 / 1 | 2,049 / 128 | +2.38% | equivalent |
| GPT-OSS 120B TP4, HW attention on | 1 / 1 | 32,769 / 128 | +4.28% | +1.03% |
| Llama 3.1 8B TP4, handwritten | 8 / 2 | 1,920 / 130 | equivalent | equivalent |
| Llama 3.1 8B TP2, handwritten | 8 / 4 | 1,920 / 130 | equivalent | equivalent |
| Llama 3.2 3B TP2, handwritten | 32 / 4 | 800 shared + 199 / 335 | equivalent | equivalent |
| Llama 3.1 8B TP2, generated | 8 / 4 | 1,920 / 130 | equivalent | equivalent |

Matched runs against main (`282955f1`) used Dice on andoria-cf8c: three isolated requests per context/version for GPT-OSS and at least 20 instance-iteration samples per version for Llama. Prompt counts include BOS where applicable. No throughput loss of 1% or more was measured in these comparisons.

Validation: `t_llama_unit`, `t_ranged_mask`, full build, formatting, and [CI host and FPGA tests](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/actions/runs/35258393447/attempts/2) pass. Tests cover Ready/Pending splits, sliding windows, query coverage, completion accounting, and cases where splitting should be declined.

title: Typed KV-cache tensors for packed V and native K (parent of #4424)
author: jhan-positron
head: c5d44bd86fe97914d2d3c7144b8045ebfad9fba0
body:
## Short version

This PR addresses the maintainer's review comments at PR #4424, model code directly work on specific data layout and it makes code hard to maintain. Issue #4525 was raised to track the issue. This PR (part of #4525) adds typed views to the KV cache, instead of bare `bf16` pointers: a typed owner and view for the VNNI packed V plane, with no public pointer constructor, and a named alias for the existing row-major view of the native K plane. The alias names the layout at the kernel boundary but does not enforce it. Stored bytes, conversions, and cache behavior stay unchanged. The KV blocks now come into existence in the call that allocates their memory, with no separate construction pass.
The change passed the machine test on delphi-3bda (identical tokens in every arm, no measurable performance change).

### Not in this PR
PR #4424 (the VNNI packed-K child) is unchanged. After merging this PR, we will rebase PR #4424 and update its code to use the new tensor data type. A distinct, enforced type for the K plane comes with that PR, where K gets its VNNI packed layout. The public API in `h/libtron.hpp` is untouched.

## Words used here

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| packed V, VNNI layout | The V plane's storage order. VNNI (Vector Neural Network Instructions) is Intel's name for the pair-interleaved operand order this layout follows. Tokens 2i and 2i+1 are interleaved value by value. One 64-byte vector load therefore holds 16 dimensions of one token pair: the even token in the low half and the odd token in the high half of each 32-bit lane. It is the B-operand layout (the right-hand matrix) of the AMX tile multiply. Address formula: `plane[(token/2)*(2*D) + 2*dim + token%2]` for D dimensions per row. |
| native K | The K plane's storage order on `main`: one row of head_size `bf16` values per token (row-major). |
| AMX, AVX-512 | Intel instruction sets. AMX is the tile matrix unit the attention kernels use for dense (fully filled) 64-token pages. AVX-512 is the 512-bit vector unit of the software path. |
| 16-lane build | `TRON_CHUNK_SIZE` is 16 (16 fp32 values per vector register, AVX-512). Since PR #4726 on `main` (merged 2026-10-01) it is the only build. The 8-lane (AVX2) build, with its row-major V, no longer exists. |
| AMX-on build, AMX-off build | Configured with `TRON_AMX_DISPATCH=ON` (the AMX kernels are compiled in) or `OFF` (they are not). CI builds AMX-on since PR #4505. Its runners have no AMX, so the kernels execute only on delphi-3bda. The AMX-off tree is a local build that checks the code compiles without the kernels. The kill switch below is a run-time setting inside an AMX-on build. |
| kill switch | `TRON_AMX_DISABLE=1`: the binary skips the AMX kernels and runs the AVX-512 software path. |
| owner, view | `v_vnni_tensor` owns one aligned V plane. `v_vnni_view` is a non-owning matrix view (rows are tokens, columns are dimensions) that holds the address formula. One element is reached through `at(token, dim)`. Whole token rows move through the bulk operations (`append_v_row`, `load_row`, `copy_token`). |
| retained slot, sliding-window slot | A KV slot is one layer's K and V storage. A retained slot keeps every token of the sequence. A sliding-window slot keeps only a recent window of tokens. |
| arena, chunk | The raw byte buffers a book allocates for its KV blocks. The accelerator cards read them directly (DMA, direct memory access). One whole-book arena holds the retained slots. Since PR #4455 on `main`, page-aligned chunks hold the sliding-window slots (PR #4456 adds the reclamation of expired chunks in the scheduler). |
| even/odd partner rule | Appending an even token also writes zeros into its odd partner's half of the pair. Appending an odd token merges into the pair and leaves the even half alone. |
| arm | One binary-plus-configuration combination under test, for example `main` with the kill switch. |
| A/B, A/A repeat | A/B: the branch binary against the `main` binary in the same configuration. A/A: the same binary and configuration run twice, as a control for run-to-run noise. |
| rc | Return code of a command; 0 means success. |

## What changes

- **`h/system/memory.hpp`**. A tag type `dma_allocation_t` (an empty type whose only job is to select an overload) and a global `void* operator new[](size_t, dma_allocation_t, std::align_val_t) noexcept` that forwards to `dma_allocate_aligned`.
  - `try_make_unique_dma_for_overwrite` now gets its memory through this `operator new[]`. Its only production caller is the KV book (`t_heap_v2` also tests it directly).
  - In C++, a call of any function named `operator new[]` implicitly creates objects in the memory it returns [N4950 (the C++23 draft standard) intro.object/13]. This covers only implicit-lifetime types, for example classes with a trivial constructor and destructor. No constructor runs, and no bytes are written.
  - Note [DMA allocation creates objects] explains the rule.
- **`h/tron/tensor/kv_cache_fwd.hpp`** (new). Forward declarations of the packed-V types, and the aliases `native_k_view<Rows, Cols>` / `const_native_k_view<Rows, Cols>` for the existing row-major `view` / `const_view` types. The aliases name the layout at the kernel signature but do not enforce it: the type is the generic row-major view, and a pointer still constructs it. The header holds no vector intrinsics. So `h/tron/kernels/amx_attn_iface.hpp` can name the typed kernel parameters and stay intrinsics-free.
- **`h/tron/tensor/v_vnni.hpp`** (new).
  - `v_vnni_tensor<Rows, Cols>`: the owner, one `bf16` array aligned to `V_PLANE_ALIGNMENT_64` bytes, trivially copyable, `as_view()` on lvalues only.
  - `v_vnni_view<T, Rows, Cols>`: the address formula, a private pointer constructor, conversion from writable to const only, bounds-checked `at(token, dim)` for one element.
  - No row type and no `expr` base. The first revision had a row expression type `v_vnni_row` and an `operator[]` that returned it. No production code used them. They were removed at the reviewer's request (review thread 4134076112, commit c12df586b6).
  - `detail::v_vnni_access`: the plane and pair-base addresses for the kernels and the bulk operations.
  - The packed operations moved here from `kv_cache.hpp` with their bodies unchanged: `append_v_row` (one token's row in, under the even/odd partner rule), `load_row` (one row out), `copy_token` (token to token).
  - Note [VNNI Packed V layout] documents the layout and the access rules.
- **`h/tron/models/kv_cache.hpp`**.
  - `kv_block::v` is a `v_vnni_tensor` with the size and alignment of the array it replaces (checked by `static_assert`).
  - `kv_block::k` is a plain `bf16` array of `page_size * head_size` values. It has the same bytes, alignment and row order as the array of `bf16s` SIMD vectors it replaces (SIMD: single instruction, multiple data. One `bf16s` fills one vector register.). `k_view` now builds its views from this array with no `reinterpret_cast`. The V reads do the same since the maintainer's PR #4698 (merge commit 8e0cf77bed): `scaled_v_expr` and `fill_storage_slot` read `bf16` arrays without a cast.
  - `page::set_v` and `page::get_v` take a typed, aligned, unit-stride row (`const_v_row_view<Source, head_size, Dma>` and `v_row_view<Destination, head_size, Dma>`, the aliases from the maintainer's PR #4697, defined in `v_vnni.hpp`) instead of a pointer.
  - `page::v_packed()` returns the const packed view of one page and KV head for the kernel.
  - `book::append` copies V through `copy_token`.
  - `scaled_v_expr` (the software path's weighted sum) takes the packed view.
  - `page::v_data` and `kv_block::v_base` are removed.
  - Note [KV block lifetime]: the `kv_block` objects in an arena or chunk come into existence at the allocation call (see `h/system/memory.hpp` above). The accessors reach them through `std::launder` (the standard function that turns an address into a pointer to the object that lives there). A plain cast of the byte address would still point at the bytes, not at the `kv_block` objects. No placement new and no second pass over the arena remain. Every block type stays trivially default-constructible, trivially copyable and trivially destructible (checked by `static_assert`). The object-creation rule of the allocation call covers only such types.
  - Note [Zero-Initialized V Slots] now names the typed operations.
- **`h/tron/models/model.hpp`**. `save_v_impl` passes the V source row as a typed view whose element type and DMA flag come from the V buffer's type.
- **`h/tron/models/self_attention.hpp`, `h/tron/kernels/amx_attn_iface.hpp`, `src/tron/kernels/amx_attn.cpp`**. `qk_rowmajor_128x4` takes `const_native_k_view<64, 128>`. `weights_times_v_128x4` takes `v_vnni_view<const bf16, 64, 128>`. The kernel bodies read the plane pointers through the typed views. The tile loads are unchanged.
- **`h/tron/scheduler/full.hpp`**. The FPGA staging callback `v_head_fn` unpacks a token's V row through `get_v` into a typed destination row.

## Response to the reviewer's comments on #4424

Here are specific points raised at #4424. Sources: the maintainer's [tensor-interface review](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4424#pullrequestreview-5270587330) and [API sketch](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4424#issuecomment-5765866077) on #4424.

| Point | In PR #4557 | Same as suggested? |
|---|---|
| Encapsulate the VNNI representation. Too many pointers say nothing about the layout they point to. | The packed V plane is reached only through an owner and a view with no public pointer. The native K plane reaches the QK kernel as a typed view. `page::v_data` and `kv_block::v_base` are removed. |
| Follow the `tensor` / `dtensor` precedent: one interface built on `expr`, so code can convert, slice and compute on any tensor type. | Dropped by agreement. The first revision gave `v_vnni_view` an `expr` base and a row expression `v_vnni_row`, so that a host tensor could be built from a packed view. No production code read the plane that way: the AMX kernel and `scaled_v_expr` read it in place, and the page methods move whole rows. The reviewer asked why the code exists (thread 4134076112). Commit c12df586b6 removes the row and the `expr` base. `v_vnni_view` is a plain struct with `at()` and the bulk operations. |
| Introduce a `vnni_tensor` type for a VNNI-packed rank-2 tensor. | `v_vnni_tensor<Rows, Cols>` for the packed V plane. |
| Give it the usual tensor operations, in particular row-wise load and store. | `append_v_row` (row in), `load_row` (row out) and `copy_token` (token to token) keep the existing vector bodies. Single elements go through `at(token, dim)`. |
| No bare `bf16_t*` (tron's `bf16`) values without an indication of the layout. | The VNNI packed V plane crosses the cache and kernel boundaries as a typed view with no public pointer constructor. A bare pointer or the K view is a compile error (tested with `STATIC_REQUIRE`). The native K plane reaches the QK kernel through `native_k_view`, an alias of the existing row-major view that names the layout but does not enforce it. A distinct K type comes with #4424. |

Summary: four of the review's five points are addressed for the planes this PR covers. The `expr` point was dropped by agreement with the reviewer. The packed-K half of each point waits for #4424. 


## Verification


### Machine test (delphi-3bda, qwen3-4b `ingested-qwen-3-4b-instruct-2507-tp2`, `runtron --instance 2,4` on cards 90:00.0 and 93:00.0 of socket 1)

The raw tables are in the first comment on this PR.

Token identity:

- Settings: greedy decoding (temperature 0, seed 1, `--pay-for-determinism`), one user with runtron's built-in prompt of the requested length (`--prompt-length`), 256 generated tokens.
- Binary: the production code of the first commit (`85084e937c`, now `b951ba9b4c`).
- Pass rule of the plan, one comparison each: branch equals `main` with AMX on; branch equals `main` with the kill switch; branch equals `main` with FPGA attention; the branch A/A repeat equals the branch. Token for token.
- Result: all 4 comparisons are identical at both prompt lengths (1024 and 8192 tokens). The branch with the kill switch also equals the branch with AMX on (AVX-512 path against AMX kernel).

Performance A/B:

- Settings: 8 users, prompt 1024 / 2048 / 8192 tokens, 256 generated tokens, 3 interleaved repetitions, 4 arms (`main` and branch, each with and without the kill switch) = 36 runs, 0 failures.
- Pass rule, fixed before the runs: every TPS and TTFT difference of the means lies inside the band.
- Band: the larger of two values. The first is 2 x the larger arm standard deviation over the 3 repetitions. The second is the reference spread measured for this shape on 2026-09-14 (0.4 TPS, 0.15 s TTFT).

| Comparison | Result |
|---|---|
| branch against `main`, AMX on: TPS and TTFT at 3 prompt lengths | 6 of 6 inside the band |
| branch against `main`, kill switch: TPS and TTFT at 3 prompt lengths | 6 of 6 inside the band |
| largest difference | +0.72 % TPS and -0.73 % TTFT, both with the branch faster |
| per-arm standard deviation | at most 0.35 TPS and 0.23 s TTFT (each under 0.5 % of its arm's mean: 71.6 TPS at prompt 1024 with the kill switch, 53.1 s TTFT at prompt 8192 with AMX on) |

Meaning: the refactor costs nothing measurable. That is the pass rule stated above.

Instruction comparison:

- Method: 19 `noinline` wrapper functions (the moved bodies and their callers) compiled against `main` and against the branch with `t_llama_unit`'s exact clang-19 command, disassembled with `objdump -d -r`, and compared after normalisation (in-function jump and call targets replaced by a placeholder, numbered string-literal labels unified, long template names shortened, so that only the instruction sequences are compared).
- Instruction-identical: the moved bodies, that is `set_v` even/odd for bf16, float and fp16, `get_v` even/odd for float and bf16, and the `scaled_v` weighted sum.
- Differ by addressing only: the `page::set_v` / `page::get_v` wrappers that take the token index at run time (one scalar `add` fewer), and the `book::append` copy closure (same vector instructions, different scalar address arithmetic).
- Allocation path: no store through the arena pointer, no `rep stos` (the x86 block-fill instruction), no `memset` and no loop.
- One difference found and removed: a bounds assert in `detail::v_vnni_access::pair_base`, which `append_v_row`, `load_row` and `copy_token` call, sat on a frequently executed path. The second commit removed it (`TRON_ASSERT` is active in release builds).
- Scope: the wrapper comparison is of the pre-rebase code. That code still had the placement-new pass.

title: Attention path stats: AVX / AMX / FPGA shares and timers behind TRON_ATTN_STATS
author: jhan-positron
head: 8c95514924767bc42360c64aadd8daa428b707ba
body:
## Short version

This PR counts how much of a model's attention work ran on each path (AVX, AMX, FPGA), and how long attention took, per layer and per pool worker (one thread of the application thread pool). 

One environment variable, `TRON_ATTN_STATS=1`, turns on the collection at run time. The numbers come out as FUSE leaves under `/model/<id>/attention/`, and as stderr summary at the end of a runtron run.

Perf impacts are neglectable. 

## Not in this PR
MoE models are not specifically scoped, it is likely MoE stats are not covered. Will add when AMX feature extends to MoE.

## Words used here

- visit: one call of `apply_page_tok`. That is one (query token, KV page of 64 tokens, KV head) triple that passed the page-level checks of `apply_page_range`. The AMX kernel serves a whole dense page per visit. The AVX loop serves the relevant K tokens of the page. An empty visit found no software work.
- forward: one model run for all users' pending token jobs. Forward class: `decode_like` when every token job has a listener (one generated token per user, but also a one-token final prompt chunk or a speculative verify step). `prompt_or_mixed` is every other forward. Under continuous batching (rinzler, the production server, adds and removes users between forwards) a forward that carries any user's prompt chunk is `prompt_or_mixed`. So `decode_like` counts pure-decode forwards only.
- listener: the consumer of one token job's logits. Every generated token has one, and so does the last token of a prompt chunk (the slice of a prompt that one forward processes). A prompt token without a listener only stores its K and V.
- pool worker: one thread of the application thread pool (`n_workers` in `summary`, 27 in the runs below). The attention workers of a forward are its last `n_attn_workers` pool workers. The first pool workers, the main helpers, do the non-attention work, and their attention rows read zero.

**Timers**, all in TSC cycles (`summary` carries `tsc_hz`):
- T1 = wall time of one model forward, taken by `forward_scope` (the one object that owns the per-forward record) inside `model::state::forward`, from just after the trace marker at its top to its return. The layers, the logits, the listener delivery and the release of the forward's synchronization latches (the latch arena) are inside. Scheduler work before and after is outside.
- T2 = busy time of one attention job on one worker. This is `attn_elapsed`, which exists today: both passes and the join, without the upstream K/V wait.
- T3 = wall time of one attention job as attention worker 0 sees it (entry to return), filed per layer. The layer and totals leaves carry the T3 and T4 keys (`wall_cycles_w0`, `period_cycles_w0` and their companions). The worker leaves do not.
- T4 = layer period on attention worker 0, filed per layer: from its first job of one attention operation to its first job of the next operation. The second minibatch of the same operation starts no period. The last layer of a forward has no period.
- T5 = `join_wait_cycles`: the time a worker spends waiting in the join with no join progress, in both join modes. In a hardware join it is the wait loop that ends when an FPGA pass or the other workers' software partials become ready. In a software-only join (CPU attention) it is the stretches of failed polls on the other workers' sections. T5 is inside T2.

## Doc and tests
Docs: `README.stats.md` describes the leaves and the switch.

Tests:

- New `t/t_attn_stats.cpp`, 17 cases. They cover tallies, rows, path sets, timers, class routing, the `forward_scope` object, the three job counts of a forward, the rows keyed by pool worker, the fold over the attention rows only, JSON leaves and their size, the leaves with the switch off, the exit report, FUSE registration with the weak_ptr rule, the last-wins takeover, and the EAGLE directory. A fork-based negative case checks that an out-of-range worker, layer or token job aborts (every hook index is a `TRON_ASSERT`). The switch rule (exactly "1") has no unit case: the reader is one function that reads the environment once, and the `TRON_ATTN_STATS=yes` runs on delphi-3bda and in the development container check the warning. The file is compiled into the `t_llama_unit` binary, so it needs no cost-data row of its own (a row needs a whole-host bench run).
- `t/t_llama_unit.cpp`: the fake-lane `apply_page_range` case asserts the stats-on tallies (32 AVX visits of 32 K tokens each, no AMX, no empty visit). The CI lane compiles without `TRON_AMX_DISPATCH`, and this case exercises the per-visit hook there. The case also reads the forward's path sets back (32 jobs `avx`, 32 jobs `none`) and checks that the visits land in the last pool row. It then repeats the call under a 2-worker split, where the same attention worker lands one row earlier. The two direct `stream_hw_joins` cases pass a real T5 accumulator and check 0. Every sweep there makes progress, so no wait is counted. After a production `apply_page_range` call, the state's own stats object is checked to follow `TRON_ATTN_STATS`.
- `t/t_amx_dispatch_dtype.cpp` asserts the amx/avx split against the kernel fakes' call counts. One section makes the fake `available()` answer false (one AVX visit that scored the whole page). After each call the path sets are read back (the AMX set exactly when the kernels ran, else the AVX set). The file also gets the `apply_page_range` argument main's copy lacks (the batch query mask). Main's copy does not compile with `-DTRON_AMX_DISPATCH=ON`, and #4557 carries the same fix.
- `t/heterogeneous_scheduler_compile.cpp`: the mixed-attention section checks the hardware join's T5 (greater than 0 and at most the join's wall time). The Q-reuse section reads T2, T3 and T4 back through `run_attention_job` (T3 includes the upstream K/V wait that a 20 ms probe makes real, T2 does not, so T3 exceeds T2). One section runs `run_joins` with no hardware plan against a producer that finishes 20 ms late, in three arms. Late producer with stats on: T5 greater than 0 and at most the wall time. Sections already done: T5 = 0. Stats flag off: T5 = 0. One section reaches `note_fpga_pass` through `prepare_hw_attention`. One case drives `model::state::forward` with the switch forced on and reads one whole record back (the class, the three job counts, T1 and the split) for a decode-like and a prompt-or-mixed forward. The fixtures that drive `apply_page_range` or `run_attention_job` with the switch on open a `forward_scope` first, as production does. This file and the direct `t_llama_unit` callers follow the `run_joins` and `stream_hw_joins` parameters.
- New `t/assertion_signal.hpp`: the fork-based helper that expects an abort, shared by `t_llama_unit.cpp`, `t_compute_attention_unit.cpp` and the negative case above (the first two had private copies).


## Why one environment variable and no CMake option

With the variable unset, a visit pays one test of a stack bool. The other hooks cost the same kind of test: three per attention job, one per failed poll and one per joined KV head in the software-only join, three per forward in `forward_scope`, and one per forward for the split. With the variable unset no hook writes memory or reads rdtsc. A visit costs est. 5,800 to 11,200 cycles (2.1 to 2.9 us per visit measured on 2026-09-01 at prompts 256 to 2048). The margin below a 1 % TPS change is therefore 60x to 400x. The A/A below is the check. 

## Off-state cost (A/A) and on-state cost

Setup: delphi-3bda, half of machine (socket 1, cards 90/93), runtron, CPU attention (`USE_HW_ATTN=0`). CPU attention is the worst case for the per-visit hooks, because every page visit is software. Model qwen-3-4b tp2, 8 users, 256 generated tokens, 3 interleaved repetitions per arm and cell. Arms: base and base2 = main 66c7bb8db1 with the variable unset (the same-binary pair gives the band). head = this branch at 9b3832eb4b with the variable unset. headon = the same binary with `TRON_ATTN_STATS=1`. TPS is the mean over the repetitions, with the sample sd. The band per cell was fixed before the runs: the largest of |base2 - base|, twice the largest per-arm sd, and 0.5 % of base.

| Cell | Arm | TPS | sd | vs base | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| prompt 1024 | base | 79.95 | 0.29 | | reference |
| prompt 1024 | base2 | 79.67 | 0.29 | -0.34 % | same binary: band 0.59 TPS (0.73 %) |

reviews.body: A few correctness and semantics issues inline, plus two design questions (forward classification; per-worker row sizing).
Approved... I think your PR description is stale at this point (after all the updates from reviews), and you currently have a merge conflict. But overall looks good.

inline.body:
T5 is only timed here, inside `stream_hw_joins` (the HW join). In SW-only layers the join waits for peer partials in the poll at `run_joins`:

```cpp
if (!join_hw && plan_state.sections_left[kv_head]) continue;  // poll
```

That spin is never timed. So on a CPU-attention run `join_wait_cycles` reads 0 even when workers are spinning on load imbalance; the `"join_wait_cycles":0` in the PR description's sample comes from exactly that config. The Note and README say T5 ends when "an FPGA pass or the other workers' software partials become ready", which suggests SW waits are included.

Either time the SW poll too (start the clock on the first `continue` for a kv head, stop when it proceeds), or narrow the docs to "HW join wait only".

replies.body:
You are right. T5 (join_wait_cycles, the join wait timer) was read only around the wait loop of stream_hw_joins, the hardware join. On a software-only join the poll on sections_left in run_joins is the only wait. Nothing timed it.

With USE_HW_ATTN=0 (the setting that keeps attention on the CPU) join_hw is false on every layer. So the 0 in the description's sample was that untimed poll, not an absence of waiting. T5 was designed as the FPGA-pass wait. The Note and README were widened when the field lost its hw_ prefix. The timing point never moved. So the text over-claimed.

Fixed in 6e23101744. run_joins now times each stretch of consecutive failed polls with no join progress in between, into the same join_wait_cycles. That costs no rdtsc read (the cycle-counter read) when the switch is off, and two reads per stretch when it is on. I chose stretches rather than one clock per KV head. With one clock per head, a worker that folds head B while head A is pending would count the fold as waiting. With stretches the fold counts as work, and the sum stays below the job's wall time.

Also added unit test to cover the missed the case.

inline.body:
Two layers write `<class>_forwards`: `forwards`, `wall_cycles` and `wall_max_cycles` come from here in `full_scheduler`, while `token_jobs`, `fpga_queries` and `token_jobs_by_path_set` come from `model::run_forward` (`begin_forward`/`end_forward`). Any other caller of `state.forward(...)` (another scheduler, a test harness, a draft path) gives `forwards == 0` next to nonzero `token_jobs`. `note_forward_wall` also relies on `current_class` having been set by `begin_forward` inside the forward.

Consider owning T1 inside `run_forward` (it can bracket logits delivery there too), or wrap begin/end/wall in one scoped helper, so a single site owns the per-forward record.

replies.body:
Agree.

Fixed in b6fd226982 with your second option, a forward_scope object in attn_stats.hpp.

It is constructed as the first statement of model::state::forward. Construction stores the class, sizes the path bits and takes the T1 start stamp. 
Destruction runs after logits, listener delivery and the latch-arena release (the per-forward scratch memory). It takes the T1 stop stamp and runs the path-set fold.
T1 (the forward wall time) stays on the span of the perfetto "forward" slice, as the design defines it.
fpga_queries keeps its writer in construct_hw_plan, inside the scope's lifetime.

inline.body:
Design question on the forward classification. It is per forward: one token job without a listener moves the whole forward, including all its decode attention, into `prompt_or_mixed`. Under rinzler continuous batching, most forwards that carry any prefill chunk are mixed, so `decode_like` would show only the pure-decode forwards and misattribute most decode attention. The runtron validation can't show this because prefill and decode forwards are separate there.

Was per-forward granularity chosen on purpose? A per-q_batch class, or tagging each token job by whether it has a listener, looks nearly free: it could be hoisted once per `apply_page_range` call like `stats_enabled`. It would answer "how much *decode* attention went to AMX/FPGA" in serving. If per-forward is intended, can the README spell out that `decode_like` means pure-decode forwards only?

replies.body:
Per-forward was deliberate as it is an important context to compare AMX and AVX.

You are right about serving. One forward walks the whole token tree. So a prefill chunk of one user shares the forward with the generated tokens of every other user, and decode_like then counts pure-decode forwards only. My previous testing used runtron only which does not have prompt and decode mixing, and I missed it. Thanks for pointing it out.

Updated in ae8a6d38d9: the README sentence you asked for, plus listener_jobs and kv_only_jobs per forward class in the _forwards leaf. With those two keys a serving reader sees how many of the prompt_or_mixed token jobs had a listener, as every generated token does.

inline.body: These range guards (`worker >= n_workers || layer >= n_layers`, and the same in `note_attn_job`, `note_join_wait`, `note_fpga_pass`, `note_token_path`) silently drop counts, and the comments say they exist for test states that grow `attn`. In production a wrong index would quietly go uncounted instead of failing. Prefer asserting (`row()` already asserts the same bounds, so the early return is also redundant) and fix the tests to build a correctly sized state. The same applies to `token_path_span` returning `nullptr` for out-of-range workers.

replies.body:
Agree.

Fixed in 15f355acb2. Every guard is a TRON_ASSERT (the assert macro, active in every build). The four hooks that go through row() lose the redundant compares. fpga_at, note_fpga_query, end_forward and token_path_span get an assert each. note_token_path had no production caller and is deleted. The per-visit bound in apply_page_range became one assert per call inside token_path_span.

inline.body:
Design question on row sizing. Rows and `path_bits` are sized by `attn.size()`, the whole app pool (27 in your run), but rows are indexed by *attention* worker index (0..`n_attn_workers`), 20 in your run. So:

- `<class>_worker_<W>` leaves exist for indices that never do attention; `active_workers` works around that.
- `end_forward` loops over all pool workers per token job, on the main thread between `plugin_state.run` and `wait_for_coop_gof`.
- If `n_attn_workers` changes between forwards, attention worker `W` maps to a different pool thread (`num_workers() - n_attn_workers + W`), so a per-worker row mixes cores over the run.

Was keying by attention worker index (instead of pool worker index) deliberate? Keying by pool worker index would make per-worker rows stable per thread/core, and the fold could skip workers with no bits set in the forward. Alternatively, record `n_attn_workers` per forward so readers can interpret the rows.

replies.body:

Fixed in bff317e0d3. The rows are keyed by pool worker index, the index the per-worker speed estimator and the perfetto "app thread id" argument already use.
T3 and T4 moved into a per-(class, layer) struct. They describe the layer, and attention worker 0 is only the observer. The worker leaves now hold per-worker values only, and `active_workers` equals `n_attn_workers_max`.

title: AMX software attention, canonical path: kernel + dispatch, default-off
author: jhan-positron
head: 85fc8ff4decf5cc278a2f0fbe23104f771f1ff5c
body:
(This is #3879 trimmed and retitled: the third of the pieces the original PR was split into. The page-share counters (instrumentation that counts how many query tokens visit each KV page; default off) are #4267; a memory order fix is #4265; this updated PR, and the K mirror re-work is to be released. The history was rebuilt as four topical commits. The pre-split head 60d66d9c04 is kept as branch `jhan-amx-p0-pre-split`.)

## Short version

This PR adds an optional AMX path to software attention. The KV page must be a full 64-token page, and the query must be allowed to use every token of it. The model must have head size 128 (128 values per head) and 4 query heads per KV head. The model must also keep its queries in bf16. For such a page, the query-key scores and the softmax-weights-times-values product are computed with AMX tile multiplies. Every other page, model shape or number format runs the existing AVX-512 loop, unchanged. 

Both paths start from the same three lookups for a page: how many tokens it holds, whether the query may use it, and the positions of the query and of the page's first token. The AVX loop made these lookups already and applies its visibility and sliding-window rules token by token, as before. The lookups now run once, before the choice between the two paths. The AMX path adds whole-page tests on them: all 64 tokens in use, one visible range, first token inside the sliding window.

The build option TRON_AMX_DISPATCH is OFF by default, and a default build compiles no AMX feature. Setting the environment variable TRON_AMX_DISABLE=1 makes the AMX build run the AVX loop on every page. That build then produces the same output values as a build without the option.

## Words used here

- **AMX**: Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions, the tile-matrix instruction set of Sapphire Rapids and later Xeons. The measurement host is a Granite Rapids Xeon 6962P.
- **KV page**: 64 tokens of K and V. **kv_mul**: query heads per KV head (grouped-query attention); the kernels serve kv_mul 4 with head size 128, hence the namespace `amx_attn_h128g4` and the `_128x4` suffix.
- **dense page**: a page whose 64 tokens are all active, visible to the query in one range, and inside the query's sliding window. Only dense pages take the AMX path.

## What changed, by commit

1. **Kernels + interface + contract document** (`src/tron/kernels/amx_attn.cpp`, `h/tron/kernels/amx_attn_iface.hpp`): the query packer, the row-major QK kernel `qk_rowmajor_128x4` (K as stored is the A operand, packed Q the B operand, the result transposed on the way out: Note [QK orientation]) and `weights_times_v_128x4`; a typed `tron::bf16` interface; the kernel bodies live in one translation unit (one .cpp file compiled on its own; the build rule that gives it the AMX flags is commit 3); the runtime switch and its contract documented.
2. **Dispatch integration** (`h/tron/models/self_attention.hpp`, `h/tron/models/kv_cache.hpp`): `is_dense_amx_page` (the predicate), apply_dense_amx_page` (QK, the same scale/max/exp step as the dotter's epilogue (the step after its dot products), PV, the accumulator update, in one function; `apply_page_tok` calls it only after two checks, that a packed Q exists and that the page is dense) and `packed_amx_query` (at most one pack per token per call, done after the outer visibility and window checks and before the dense predicate); the raw V accessors `page::v_data` / `kv_block::v_base`. The dotter loop and its arithmetic are unchanged; the begin/end/position/visibility prologue it used moved above the dispatch so both paths share it.
3. **Build option + CI flag** (`CMakeLists.txt`, `src/tron/CMakeLists.txt`, `.github/workflows/cmake-single-platform.yml`, `README.ci.md`): `option(TRON_AMX_DISPATCH)` in the top-level `CMakeLists.txt`; when ON, `src/tron/CMakeLists.txt` adds the kernel source with the AMX compiler flags on that one file only. The CMake CI lane configures with the option ON, so the kernels and the dispatch compile whenever that lane's build step runs (a cached build artifact can skip it). The kernel cases of `t_amx_numerics` execute tile instructions only when the runtime check `available()` passes (an AMX CPU with OS tile support, in practice a Granite Rapids runner); elsewhere they print a warning and return. The workflow does not require a real-AMX execution for every candidate tip; that remains open (issue #3997).
4. **Tests** (`t/CMakeLists.txt`, `t/t_amx_numerics.cpp`, `t/t_amx_dispatch_dtype.cpp`, `t/t_llama_unit.cpp`, `config/test-benchmarks.json`): `t_amx_numerics` (the compile-time eligibility gate over the executors' activation scalars and the shape; packer layout compared bit for bit; QK against the AVX dotter within the fp32 add-order envelope; PV within the round-to-nearest versus truncation envelope), `t_amx_dispatch_dtype` (the production dispatch with CPU fakes, stand-in definitions of every kernel entry point that record their calls and run no AMX instruction: a bf16 executor packs once and calls QK and PV once for a full page; a 63-token page packs but calls neither kernel; float and fp16 executors never reach the fakes). `t/t_llama_unit.cpp` only swaps a literal 2 for the new named constant `KV_BLOCK_PLANES_2`; the eligibility case the original PR added there was dropped, because the first case of `t_amx_numerics` checks the same predicate.

Why these tests: the numerics test fails at compile time if the eligibility gate admits a float or fp16 activation scalar or a shape other than head 128 with 4 query heads per KV head, and at run time if the packer misplaces a value or if a kernel's result leaves the error envelope its inputs allow (fp32 add order for QK, the weight rounding mode for PV), which is the contract the dispatch relies on. The dispatch test fails if the type gate lets a float or fp16 executor reach the packer or if the dense predicate lets its 63-token page reach the kernels; it checks call counts and the captured query values, not attention outputs. The two tests protect different boundaries; both are cheap host tests, and the kernel cases need an AMX host.

## Review items from the first round

The seven inline comments Ben left on the canonical path have responses in the code and the document; a comment-by-comment map (old comment, new file and symbol, what changed) is the first comment below this description. Jeremy's two comments from Codex, the automated reviewer he ran (lazy setup; aligned pack buffer) keep the answers and measurements given on 2026-08-31; the pack buffer is `alignas(64)` storage of `tron::bf16` (the old head had aligned `uint16_t`).

## Evidence

All measurements were taken on delphi-3bda (Intel Xeon 6962P, a Granite Rapids CPU) with attention in software (USE_HW_ATTN=0). Words used: "clean" is a build made without the option; the "kill switch" is the AMX build run with TRON_AMX_DISABLE=1; an "arm" is one of these settings under comparison; a "placement" is the set of FPGA cards, CPU cores and NUMA node a run is pinned to.

There are two kinds of measurement. The runtron measurements compare two builds, the AMX build against a clean build, and their tokens/s are per user (each request's own rate in the runtron log). The nightly system tests compare one binary run twice, with and without the kill switch.

### runtron: qwen-3-4b tp2, 8 users, prompt 8192 tokens

**August measurement (2026-08-19).** Pre-split binaries, on cards 10:00.0 and 13:00.0 (socket 0). Decode was 14.50 tokens/s per user with the clean build and 17.04 with AMX, a gain of +17.5%. Prefill was 65.4 tokens/s per request clean and 124.5 with AMX, +90.5%.

**Repeat 1 (2026-09-07, shared machine, socket 1).** The same workload on commit 9723d56f62, whose code is this PR's. The machine was shared during this repeat, so the placement changed from August's: instance 2,4 on cards 90:00.0 and 93:00.0 (socket 1), with the application and device core numbers shifted by 72 and NUMA node 1 instead of 0. All three arms used this one placement. So the absolute tokens/s are not comparable with August's, but the AMX gain is: +17.7% here against +17.5% in August. The run was done twice; the two rounds agreed to 0.07 tokens/s (clean) and 0.001 tokens/s (AMX).

| Arm (Repeat 1, mean of two rounds) | Decode, tokens/s per user | Prefill time per 8192-token request (eight at once) | Prefill throughput per request, tokens/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| clean | 14.65 | about 122 s | 67.0 |
| kill switch | 14.75 (within 0.7% of clean; 0.8% and 0.5% in the two rounds) | about 122 s | 67.1 |
| AMX | 17.25 (+17.7%) | 53.6 s | 152.8 (+128%) |

The prefill gain, about +128%, is larger than August's +90.5%. These measurements do not separate the effect of the code change from the effects of the new placement and the shared host. Raw log: exec/results/qwen8u8k-pr1-half-20260907T1904.txt in the campaign repository.

**Repeat 2 (2026-09-07, free machine, August's placement).** Later the same day (21:15 to 21:31 UTC) the machine was free, and the same workload and commit were run again in August's placement: instance 0,4 on cards 10:00.0 and 13:00.0, socket 0, the same core lists as in August. Two rounds again.

| Arm (Repeat 2) | Decode round 1 | Decode round 2 | Decode mean | Prefill time per request | Prefill throughput per request |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| clean | 14.662 | 14.682 | 14.67 | 122.1 s | 67.1 tokens/s |
| kill switch | 14.795 | 14.764 | 14.78 (+0.7%) | 122.0 s | 67.2 tokens/s |
| AMX | 17.292 | 17.278 | 17.285, written 17.29 (+17.8%) | 53.6 s | 152.9 tokens/s (+128%, the same as on socket 1) |

Decode is tokens/s per user. With the placement equal to August's, the AMX decode gain (+17.8%) matches August's (+17.5%), and the absolute rates are within 1.5% of August's: 14.67 against 14.50 clean, 17.29 against 17.04 with AMX. Raw log: exec/results/qwen8u8k-pr1-20260907T1904.txt in the campaign repository.

### Nightly system tests, re-run 2026-09-04

One binary, run with and without the kill switch. These binaries were built before the rebase and before this split. 8 users, prompt about 1,024 tokens.

| Model and metric | Kill switch (AMX off) | AMX on | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| llama-3.1-8b tp2, decode tokens/s per user | 76.07 | 86.66 | +13.9% |
| qwen-3-4b tp4, decode tokens/s per user | 77.83 | 81.37 | +4.5% |
| qwen-3-4b tp4, TTFT (time to first token) | 1,777 ms | 1,618 ms | -8.9% |
| qwen-3-4b tp4, MMLU Pro accuracy | 66.14% | 67.64% | +1.5 points, smaller than the 1.7 points between two unchanged runs of the AMX-off arm |


### Verification of this tip

Built and tested on 2026-09-07 on delphi-3bda (Intel Xeon 6962P, a Granite Rapids CPU).

The build used commit 9723d56f62 in a clean worktree. This PR's tip fcc7857 differs from that commit only in the cost-data file config/test-benchmarks.json, which no test reads.

CMake preset: cross-avx512, with -DBUILD_INGEST_MODELS=OFF (this only skips the ingest models). The tree was built twice: once with -DTRON_AMX_DISPATCH=ON and once with -DTRON_AMX_DISPATCH=OFF, the option's default. In both builds the three test targets and the tron library they link compiled.

Test results, as printed by Catch2 (the test framework):

| Test | Option ON | Option OFF (default build) |
|---|---|---|
| t_amx_numerics | All tests passed (4109 assertions in 4 test cases) | skip stub: All tests passed (1 assertion in 1 test case) |
| t_amx_dispatch_dtype | All tests passed (1559 assertions in 1 test case) | skip stub: All tests passed (1 assertion in 1 test case) |
| t_llama_unit | All tests passed (120054 assertions in 27 test cases) | All tests passed (120054 assertions in 27 test cases) |

With the option ON, t_amx_numerics printed no "AMX unavailable" warning. So its two kernel test cases ran real AMX tile instructions on this CPU.

The whole pre-split tree, rebased onto the same base commit, passed the same three tests with the option ON on 2026-09-06. That tree is the reference the split is checked against.

clang-format-19, the repository's formatter, leaves the files of this PR unchanged.

CI's "Check slice cost data" step requires a time and memory entry for every test. The entries for the two new tests were measured on the same host with bin/slice bench --update, at the 1-, 2- and 4-slot placements, and are part of commit 4:

| Test | Time (s), 1 / 2 / 4 slots | Memory (MB), 1 / 2 / 4 slots |
|---|---|---|

## Subsequent PR
Separate changes will add the following features:
- gpt-oss 120B and 20B on AMX
- MoE router matrix calculations use AMX

title: Free and repopulate GOF staging buffers after DMA completion (Story 2814)
author: jhan-positron
head: 576843b189e9803f0fc48fc4483ff7a62012a461
body:
Treat each gof's two 8 KB hwcacheblock staging buffers (k.data/v.data) as a reconstructable cache: free them once every in-flight DMA that reads them has completed, and rebuild on demand (reacquire + rebuild position tables + repopulate from the host KV pages) when a later submission needs the GOF. The durable copies remain the host books and device HBM, so the free is a cache eviction -- GOF identity (gal.gofs[layer], gof_job refs, shard state) is unchanged. See Note [GOF staging eviction].

Interface / behavior:
- gof: add dma_inflight (atomic) + staging_mutex, prepare_for_dma() (reacquire + populate + reserve a credit under the mutex before xfer_gof), free_staging_if_idle() (frees both buffers once dma_inflight hits 0), and the inflight_guard RAII credit (commit() after xfer_gof keeps it).
- hwcacheblock: alloc_buffer/release_buffer/clear/is_allocated; k/v gain non-virtual rebuild_positions()/reacquire_buffer() (no new pos virtuals).
- pending_xfer: add pinned_gof (shared_ptr<gof>) pinning staging for the life of its in-flight DMA and serving as the dma_inflight decrement target.
- dma_tracker::push() is now noexcept (a post-submit failure terminates rather than unwinding into a free-under-DMA); poll_completions decrements and frees outside dma_tracker::mu to avoid a staging_mutex<->mu lock-order inversion.
- Submission sites gof_rodeo_impl and backfill_shard route through prepare_for_dma / commit / push.

Tests:
- t_dma_tracker (pos_fake): staging lifecycle, inflight_guard, poll-frees-after- last, clear-drops-pin, prepare/free allocation-neutrality.
- t_gof_dma (FPGA): free -> reacquire -> fill -> xfer -> readback; and prepare_for_dma reacquire/populate/credit.
- t_gof_staging_leaks (FPGA, new): real DMA-heap allocation-balance leak suite across submit/track/complete/free + multi-device fanout.

Validated: make build-test clean; t_dma_tracker 33/1718; t_gof_dma and t_gof_staging_leaks pass on FPGA (slice-scoped); make format + lint clean.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **High Risk**
> Changes DMA staging lifetime, concurrent free vs submit paths, and lock ordering; bugs could use-after-free staging under live DMA or corrupt GOF state.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Story 2814** treats each GOF’s two 8 KB `hwcacheblock` staging buffers as a **reconstructable cache**: after HBM DMA completes, `dma_tracker::poll_completions` can evict them via `gof::free_staging_if_idle`; the next transfer uses `prepare_for_dma` to reallocate, rebuild `positions` tables, and repopulate from host KV pages.
> 
> The lifecycle is guarded by **`dma_inflight`**, **`staging_mutex`**, and **`inflight_guard`**: credit is reserved before `xfer_gof`, **`commit()`** after descriptors are live, and **`pending_xfer::pinned_gof`** keeps the GOF (and staging) alive until completion decrements the last credit. **`dma_tracker::push` is `noexcept`** so post-submit failures terminate instead of freeing staging under active DMA; staging frees run **outside** the tracker mutex to avoid lock inversion with `staging_mutex`.
> 
> **`gof_rodeo_impl`** and **`backfill_shard`** share this path. **`clear()`** remains an abandon-only shutdown hook and does not treat queue drain as completion.
> 
> Tests cover fake lifecycle (`t_dma_tracker`), FPGA round-trip/reacquire (`t_gof_dma`), and a new FPGA leak suite (`t_gof_staging_leaks`).
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 576843b189e9803f0fc48fc4483ff7a62012a461. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>
